newsitem.title: cambodia: Ung Huot appointed Cambodia's first premier.
newsitem.headline: Ung Huot appointed Cambodia's first premier.

text.p: Foreign Minister Ung Huot was formally appointed Cambodia's first prime minister on Thursday after King Norodom Sihanouk dropped his opposition to the replacement of his son, Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
The ailing Sihanouk sent a message from Peking earlier on Thursday saying acting head of state Chea Sim could issue a decree replacing Ranariddh, who was overthrown in a bloody coup on July 6.

"His Excellency Ung Huot is the first prime minister of the royal government of the Kingdom of Cambodia instead of (His Majesty) Prince Norodom Ranariddh," Chea Sim said in a decree read over national radio and television.
Powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who overthrew Ranariddh, backed Ung Huot's nomination and it was approved by parliament on Wednesday.
Ung Huot will lead the royalist FUNCINPEC party in a power-sharing coalition with Hun Sen. The coalition was set up in 1993 after a U.N.-supervised election won by the royalists.
The U.S. Embassy in Phnom Penh said the parliament's vote in favour of Ung Huot on Wednesday was undemocratic given the climate of intimidation in the country following Ranariddh's ouster.

Sihanouk, who is required by the constitution to approve a new first prime minister, made no mention of his personal approval for Ung Huot's appointment but told Chea Sim in a brief message that he should sign the decree appointing Ung Huot if he thought it appropriate.

"If, in your understanding it should be, you can sign that decree of appointment," the king told Chea Sim in a message from Beijing where Sihanouk is receiving medical treatment. A copy of the message was released by the palace in Phnom Penh.

Ranariddh was ousted after two days of battles in Phnom Penh between troops loyal to the rival prime ministers. Sihanouk said soon after he would not sign any decrees on behalf of the new government but he authorised Chea Sim to do so.

He later said he would not recognise Ung Huot as first premier as the post belonged to his son. The king also said that a vote on a new first prime minister by an incomplete parliament would be invalid.
Ung Huot said earlier on Thursday that he, Hun Sen and Chea Sim would travel to Beijing on Monday for a meeting with Sihanouk the following day. "He will be blessing us," Ung Huot said.
In Tokyo the second vice-president of the Cambodian parliament said earlier he did not approve of its election of Ung Huot to replace the prince.
"A session of the National Assembly under the threat of weapons to me is not valid," Son Soubert said in a lecture in Tokyo. "I do not agree with the appointment of the new prime minister."

Son Soubert was among some 20 members of parliament from FUNCINPEC and a small allied party who fled from the country in the wake of Hun Sen's bloody July 6 take-over and a subsequent crackdown on the opposition in which some 40 people were killed, according to United Nations human rights officials.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi told reporters in Kuala Lumpur that Ung Huot's approval by parliament was a "heartening" development but a U.S. Embassy official in Phnom Penh said it was not democratic given the atmosphere of intimidation in Cambodia.

"While we respect Ung Huot as an individual, in the absence of a return by FUNCINPEC members of parliament in exile, and in the current atmosphere of intimidation we do not believe yesterday's votes were democratic," an embassy spokesperson told Reuters.
"We hope that FUNCINPEC will revisit this issue when a genuinely free and open environment returns to Phnom Penh," the spokesperson said.
But Ung Huot dismissed the U.S. concern saying 99 of the assembly's 120 members, and more than 80 percent of FUNCINPEC members, attended the assembly session which approved his nomination.
"If anyone says this is not democratic I say think again," Ung Huot told a news conference.

A delegation of human rights activists from five Southeast Asian nations said in Bangkok on Thursday that a climate of fear prevailed in Cambodia, more than a month after the coup and the international community must push to ensure that human rights are respected.
